items.title: Claude’s new rules against game cloning won’t stop the AI copying boom
items.description: Last week, Anthropic introduced a new system prompt designed to stop its Claude models from re-creating specific, existing video games. While that move could help shield Anthropic from some liability, it's unlikely to slow much of the massive wave of AI-assisted game porting and copying that has emerged in recent months. A social media user and AI decompilation enthusiast going by the name "chasm" was among the first to note the prompt change late last week, saying a new rule seemed to be added to the Claude Code prompt on or around October 27. That rule—included in a json file under the name "tengu_heron_brook"—reads as follows: Do build original games, games in a genre, and games from the user’s own designs and assets. Don’t build a recreation of a specific existing game, even if it is renamed or called original. XDA later independently verified that the new rule appears in version 2.1.314 of the Claude Code binary, which was released on October 30 . XDA also reported that the "tengu_heron_brook" rule had been used for other purposes in earlier versions and that the Claude Opus 5.5 model specifically seemed to have its own distinct and independent instructions restricting game recreations as part of its system prompt bundle. items.title: Prepare web content for Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases with Crawl4AI
items.description: When you build Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) applications, answer quality depends on the data that you ingest. Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases is the fully managed RAG capability of Amazon Bedrock. With Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Base , you connect your data sources, and Amazon Bedrock manages ingestion, storage, indexing, and retrieval for you. You don’t provision or scale a vector store, and embedding and reranking use service-managed models by default. For web content, start with the Amazon Bedrock Web Crawler data source connector for managed knowledge bases. You give it the seed URLs or sitemaps that you’re authorized to crawl, and it crawls within the scope and rate limits that you set. Scheduled syncs keep your knowledge base current as pages change, and the connector can wait for content that loads with JavaScript. There’s no crawler for you to build, host, or operate, so this connector is the starting point for most public website content. Some sources need more control over what reaches the knowledge base. You might want to index only the main content region of each page, remove navigation and other boilerplate, or attach your own metadata attributes to every document. For that class of source material, you can extend the reach of your knowledge base with a preparation step built with Crawl4AI , an open source Python crawler. The step writes Markdown and a metadata sidecar for each page to Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3), and the knowledge base ingests both through its Amazon S3 data source. In this post, we show you how to choose the appropriate web ingestion path and implement custom preparation for content that needs additional processing. You then start ingestion into a managed knowledge base and validate retrieval quality. The companion aws-samples repository provides the complete workflow as a sample implementation. This is batch ingestion of known web properties, not real-time web access at inference time such as Web Grounding with Amazon Nova. Solution overview Start with the Amazon Bedrock Web Crawler when it can reach and index the pages you need. It respects robots.txt , and after the first full crawl, each sync captures only added, updated, and deleted content. Use the Crawl4AI preparation path when public source material needs one or more of the following before ingestion: Structured Markdown preparation : Use DefaultMarkdownGenerator with a pruning content filter to reduce navigation and other boilerplate while preserving headings, lists, and tables. Because pruning is heuristic, review representative output from your sites. Bounded, targeted extraction : Extract only the page region that an optional CSS selector matches. Constrain breadth-first traversal by seed origin, page/path/host scope, depth and page caps, and URL patterns. Custom metadata : Attach source URLs, crawl timestamps, content type, and your own attributes to each document, so that you can filter retrieval results on them. Because managed and customer-managed knowledge bases both support Amazon S3 data sources, the Crawl4AI path works with either type. This post uses a managed knowledge base and notes where a customer-managed knowledge base differs. The rest of this post follows the companion sample. Treat its architecture and defaults as a starting point, not as requirements of Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases. By default, the sample runs the AWS Fargate task in a public subnet, where it reaches your configured websites through an internet gateway. Crawl4AI’s role ends once it has prepared the source documents and metadata sidecars. From ingestion onward, Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases handles parsing, chunking, embedding, indexing, and retrieval. The following diagram shows the Crawl4AI path from the schedule through to retrieval. Figure 1: The Crawl4AI-to-Amazon S3 ingestion path for Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases The numbered steps in the diagram map to the following workflow: Amazon EventBridge starts the Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) task on AWS Fargate on the configured schedule. The task crawls the public websites you configured and prepares Markdown with a metadata sidecar for each page. The task uploads the prepared files to the Amazon S3 bucket that backs the knowledge base data source. The task starts an Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases ingestion job. Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases reads the new and changed objects, parses them, and applies the chunking strategy you selected. It creates embeddings and indexes them in the knowledge base’s vector store, which Amazon Bedrock manages for a managed knowledge base. Your generative AI application queries the knowledge base for relevant chunks or for a generated response with citations. The task reads its non-secret pipeline configuration from AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store at startup. The workflow processes public pages only and doesn’t implement authenticated sessions. For sites that require sign-in, evaluate the Amazon Bedrock Web Crawler authentication options first, which include basic, form-based, and SAML authentication. Extending the sample with authentication requires session handling, credentials in AWS Secrets Manager, and a security review. How the workflow works The AWS Cloud Development Kit (AWS CDK) app packages the implementation in a container image during deployment. When the schedule fires, the container runs scripts/container_entrypoint.py and executes crawl, upload, and ingestion in sequence. The following three steps explain the core logic. Step 1: Crawl and extract content The crawl step performs bounded crawling and writes a Markdown file with a metadata sidecar for each successfully prepared page. The following excerpt is simplified. The module src/crawl4ai_bedrock_kb/crawl.py contains the complete seed pacing, URL filtering and scoping, page limits, and redirect checks: async def crawl_and_prepare(config: PipelineConfig, output_dir: str) -> list[str]: written, seen = [], set() pa

items.title: Build efficient agents with knowledge distillation on Amazon SageMaker AI
items.description: You built a shopping assistant on a frontier model, and it works. A shopper asks for “a black waist bag under twenty dollars from a shop with at least 4.5 stars,” and the agent searches the catalog, inspects candidates, checks the constraints, and commits to a recommendation. But what does that interaction actually cost? An agentic assistant is not one model call, it is a loop: search, read results, refine, verify, decide. A single completed task can be multiple calls to that frontier model, and you pay for every one, on every shopper. At production scale, that per-task cost compounds, erodes the project’s ROI, and stops the project from shipping. One way to make an agentic application more efficient is to use a smaller model, which is faster to respond and more cost-effective to host. The catch is quality: a smaller model usually falls short on the task, which is why the larger one was chosen in the first place. Knowledge distillation closes that gap by transferring the behavior of the larger “teacher” model into a smaller “student”, training the student to reproduce the teacher’s outputs, so it keeps much of the quality at the smaller model’s speed and cost. In this post you will learn how to use knowledge distillation, and specifically sequence-level knowledge distillation (SeqKD), to fine-tune a shopping agent on Amazon SageMaker AI . We cover how to generate high-quality multi-step trajectories with a frontier teacher and keep the ones that solve the task, how to encode them for supervised fine-tuning, how to run the training on serverless infrastructure, and how to evaluate the student against a held-out benchmark. Figure 1: One agentic task is a loop, not a single call: the agent searches, reads results, refines, verifies, and decides, and each step is a separate billed call to the frontier model. A single completed task can be multiple calls, on every shopper What is sequence-level knowledge distillation (SeqKD)? The simplest applicable form of distillation is sequence-level knowledge distillation (SeqKD). It uses a teacher model to generate high-quality responses, then trains a student model on those responses with supervised fine-tuning (SFT). SeqKD needs only the teacher’s text , with no access to teacher logits and no reinforcement-learning infrastructure, so it works even with a closed or API-only teacher. Compared to other approaches such as logit-based or on-policy, it sits at the most cost-effective and portable end of the distillation spectrum. The teacher writes the answers, and the student is fine-tuned on them. Because those answers persist as a dataset, you can reuse them to train or test different students without regenerating the data. In principle, you would want the student to match the teacher’s full distribution over possible outputs. The caveat here is that you can’t. The space of possible sequences is astronomically large, so matching it exactly isn’t feasible. SeqKD sidesteps that by approximating it with samples the teacher actually produces. For an agent, the sequence the teacher produces is not a block of prose but a trajectory, an ordered run of reasoning, tool calls, and the observations they return, where each step is conditioned on everything before it. Training the student on that whole sequence teaches it the reasoning that leads to each action and the multi-step course of action itself, not a single paragraph of answer text. That makes an agentic task one of the cleanest illustrations of sequence-level KD, because the sequence being copied is the behavior itself. Figure 2: SeqKD transfers behavior through the teacher’s text outputs alone: the teacher generates trajectories, the student trains on them, and the result keeps much of the teacher’s quality at the small model’s speed and cost. No teacher weights, logits, or gradients are required during training, so it runs as ordinary supervised fine-tuning When SeqKD is the right choice SeqKD fits a specific set of situations: You have the inputs but no high-quality target outputs This is the core case for SeqKD, which is fundamentally data generation. You supply the inputs, and the teacher writes the targets, so you can fine-tune on a task or domain that has no existing high-quality labels. The targets can be as simple as single answers or as involved as multi-turn tool-use trajectories. This post takes the demanding end of that spectrum, agentic trajectories, which are especially hard to source. A single task branches into many partially correct runs, and telling a solved run from a failed one takes a reliable grader. A benchmark with a programmatic scorer supplies exactly that, so you can let the teacher generate trajectories and keep only the ones that solve the task. Your teacher is a frontier model you can only reach through an API This is the normal case for frontier models. You can’t access the weights to host it yourself, you can’t read its logits, and you can’t fine-tune it. That rules out logit-based distillation and on-policy methods, which all need that internal access. SeqKD needs only the teacher’s text responses, so it is the one approach that still works, and it frees you from paying frontier prices on every request after the student takes over. You want a strong, cost-effective first step Some of the strongest small reasoning models were built in significant part with SeqKD (supervised fine-tuning on teacher reasoning traces), so it is an effective starting point for reasoning transfer when the setup is right. The DeepSeek-R1 distilled models are a well-known example: the reasoning of a large teacher was distilled into smaller Qwen and Llama students by fine-tuning them on the teacher’s generated reasoning traces. items.title: Agentic engineering intelligence with Amazon Nova Multimodal Embeddings and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
items.description: When a qualified aerospace component goes obsolete or hits a long lead time, an engineer spends days cross-referencing specifications across vendor datasheets, interface control documents (ICDs), and qualification records before documenting a substitution justification for review. An incorrect substitution on a flight-critical component can cause mission failure, yet the evidence trail behind each decision is often spread across email and undocumented institutional knowledge, so there is no formal, repeatable package for a reviewer to check. A previous post, Manufacturing intelligence with Amazon Nova Multimodal Embeddings , showed how the model retrieves answers locked inside engineering diagrams, thermal plots, and datasheet charts that text-only pipelines miss. This post picks up where that retrieval work left off, putting those capabilities inside a multi-agent system that assembles substitution evidence, from retrieval to a drafted assessment. In this post, we show how to build a multi-agent engineering assistant that cuts the manual cross-referencing behind part substitution evaluation using Amazon Bedrock AgentCore , Amazon Nova Multimodal Embeddings , and the open source Strands Agents SDK . A planner routes work across three specialist agents that search a multimodal knowledge base, score candidates against deterministic tolerance rules, compare part photos, and ground lifecycle claims in live web data. The engineer remains the decision-maker throughout, because the system assembles evidence and drafts documents without ever approving a substitution on its own. Solution overview The assistant is built around one design rule, which is that the engineer makes every decision and the system assembles the evidence for it. That rule determines where we use large language models (LLMs) and where we use deterministic code instead. Three pillars define the architecture: Deterministic spec-fit evaluation – Tolerance-rule code written in Python scores each candidate part against the reference part and the engineer’s stated requirements. Because the same inputs consistently produce the same pass/flag verdicts, the results can go into a formal engineering review. Multi-agent orchestration – A lightweight planner routes each query to one or more of three specialist agents (Catalog, Evaluation, Knowledge), and a supervisor synthesizes their findings only when more than one specialist contributed. Complex questions such as “Check if this wheel is going end-of-life, find alternatives, and score them” chain all three specialists in sequence. Human-in-the-loop decision – The system drafts justification memos and Integration Impact Assessments for engineering review, but it doesn’t recommend or approve a substitution. Every evaluation also writes an audit trail entry aligned with AS9100 sections 8.4 and 8.5.6. The following diagram shows the architecture. Figure 1: Architecture of the multi-agent engineering assistant on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Amazon Bedrock AgentCore is a platform to build, connect, and optimize agents at scale, with any framework or model. In this solution, chat requests from the engineer’s application flow into a multi-agent graph hosted on AgentCore runtime: a planner (Claude Haiku 5.5) produces a routing plan, specialists (Claude Sonnet 5.5) execute their tools, and a supervisor (Claude Opus 5.5) synthesizes their results when more than one specialist ran. The specialists retrieve from a managed knowledge base that we created with Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Bases using Amazon Nova Multimodal Embeddings, routed through an AgentCore Gateway, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, alongside the Web Search connector for live web data. For image-as-query (uploading a chart to identify a part), the agent calls a native Amazon S3 Vectors index directly, because the managed knowledge base retrieval API doesn’t accept image input. Amazon S3 Vectors is a capability of Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3). A separate fixed chain (Knowledge, then Evaluation, then Supervisor) produces the formal Integration Impact Assessment (IIA) document. Amazon Nova Multimodal Embeddings appears in two distinct roles: Multimodal retrieval – Datasheets, ICDs, and performance charts are embedded with Nova Multimodal Embeddings so text and visual content share one semantic space. An engineer can enter “torque curve for the 0.06 Nms wheel” or upload a chart image, and retrieval returns the matching diagram with source attribution. Visual similarity scoring – When two candidate parts are compared, Nova Multimodal Embeddings produces a quantitative cosine similarity between their photos, and Claude analyzes the specific physical differences (mounting pattern, connector placement, housing geometry). The score adds supporting evidence to the deterministic spec comparison, which is what the fit verdict is based on. Prerequisites To follow along, you need: An AWS account with access to Amazon Bedrock in the US East (N. Virginia) AWS Region. Model access to Amazon Nova Multimodal Embeddings, Claude Haiku 5.5, Claude Sonnet 5.5, and Claude Opus 5.5 in Amazon Bedrock. For model availability by Region, see Model support by AWS Region in Amazon Bedrock . A managed knowledge base created with Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Bases, using Amazon Nova Multimodal Embeddings over your parts corpus (datasheets, ICDs, descriptions) for text and document retrieval. An Amazon S3 Vectors index over your part photos and datasheet chart crops, for the image-as-query path. An Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway with the Web Search connector and a managed knowledge base target. Python 3.10 or later and Jupyter for running the notebooks. items.title: How Circle K accelerated DevOps incident triage to under 15 minutes with Amazon Bedrock
items.description: This post was co-written with Marek Klatowicz, Cloud DevOps Engineer at Circle K. Many DevOps teams know the incident triage pattern: An alert fires, and before anyone can fix the problem, an engineer spends 45–60 minutes figuring out what happened. They pull logs, check service health, and correlate symptoms across a handful of tools. All of this happens before remediation can begin. At Circle K, this challenge scaled with the business. The company operates more than 17,200 convenience and fuel retail stores across 27 countries. Behind the storefronts, a cloud-native infrastructure supports point-of-sale systems, loyalty applications, and electric vehicle (EV) charging applications running on AWS. As the company expanded its digital operations, the triage overhead grew with it. More services meant more alerts, and each one required the same manual investigation before remediation could begin. To address it, Circle K built an automated triage system using Amazon Bedrock , a fully managed service that makes foundation models (FMs) available through a single API. For model availability by AWS Region, refer to Supported models by AWS Region in Amazon Bedrock . The system uses an agentic AI architecture to investigate each incident autonomously and deliver a structured summary to Slack within minutes of an alert firing. Instead of raw alerts, on-call engineers now receive actionable context, so they can act immediately rather than spending an hour figuring out what happened. Since deploying this system, Circle K has reduced mean triage time to under 15 minutes, a 67–75 percent reduction based on the team’s internal incident-response metrics. In this post, we describe the architecture for both the initial Amazon Bedrock Flows implementation and the migration to Amazon Bedrock AgentCore , and share lessons learned from scaling the system. The challenge of triage overhead Circle K’s DevOps team monitors infrastructure across multiple AWS accounts using Grafana. A typical day brings alerts for container restarts, elevated error rates, latency spikes, and failed deployments. Each alert is a useful signal, but as the system expanded, the team wanted to help on-call engineers quickly see which signals needed attention, with the right context. When an alert came in, the triage involved a familiar sequence of manual steps: reviewing recent logs in Amazon CloudWatch , examining application-level traces in Amazon OpenSearch Service , checking Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) task status, and cross-referencing symptoms with internal runbooks in GitHub. This gave engineers the information they needed, but it also showed how much repetitive context gathering would be required as more services were onboarded. The team recognized two areas where a proactive investment could help. First, the same log queries, health checks, and runbook lookups would be repeated for every incident. Second, the depth and speed of triage could vary with the on-call engineer’s familiarity with the affected service. As alert volume and service ownership grew, switching between multiple tools for each investigation could slow response and make it harder to apply the team’s best practices consistently. Circle K’s DevOps team therefore started a research and development (R&D) initiative to explore how AI could support monitoring and incident triage. The goal was to automate repetitive context gathering and provide structured, actionable findings, while supporting engineers’ operational judgment during an investigation. Why Circle K chose Amazon Bedrock The team evaluated several approaches before building, including open source agent frameworks on self-managed infrastructure. That approach would have meant owning model hosting, prompt versioning, tool orchestration, and security controls. With Amazon Bedrock, the team avoided that overhead. They could access foundation models through a single API and swap foundation models without rewriting code. Because Circle K already ran on AWS, Amazon Bedrock fit into existing AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) policies, Amazon Virtual Private Cloud (Amazon VPC) configurations, and logging pipelines. Two managed capabilities covered orchestration and retrieval. Amazon Bedrock helped with agent orchestration, giving the agents native tool use to call AWS APIs, query databases, and retrieve documents without custom orchestration code. Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases, the fully managed Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) capability, handled ingestion and retrieval of internal product cards, so the team did not need to run a separate vector database. This let the DevOps team focus on prompt design and tool definitions. Data privacy completed the picture. Circle K’s incident data includes operational metrics, infrastructure details, and logs that can contain sensitive information. Amazon Bedrock does not share customer data with model providers or use it to train foundation models . For a team feeding production logs and internal service details into the system, this data handling approach met Circle K’s security requirements. Solution overview This section describes the initial architecture, which the team built on Amazon Bedrock Flows. A later section covers the migration to AgentCore. The solution uses Amazon Bedrock Flows as the orchestration layer, coordinating a set of specialized agents that each handle a different part of the analysis. The pipeline starts when a Grafana alert publishes a notification to Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS) , which forwards it to an Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) queue. An AWS Lambda function polls the queue, extracts the alert payload, and invokes the Flow. Inside the Flow, two agents are invoked in parallel. The AWSResourceExplorerAgent queries infrastructure across multiple workload accounts managed with AWS Organizations . It checks Amazon ECS task status, Application Load Balancer target health, and CloudWatch metr

items.title: Raising the quality of insights in agentic analytics
items.description: In just a few years, generative AI has changed the face of enterprise analytics, notably by making analytics accessible to users across the organization. Agentic AI promises to do even more, by automating entire workflows and taking actions based on agent insights. But there is a problem: The quality of insights that agents currently generate leaves much to be desired. Fewer than half of agent-generated insights at the organizations surveyed for this report lead to business improvement. And while most respondents praise the quality of their agents’ descriptive insights, reviews of their prescriptive insights—those on which actions are based—are decidedly mixed. DOWNLOAD THE REPORT Failure to produce insights that improve the business deprives organizations of their desired return on investment in agentic analytics. Worse, flawed insights that trigger incorrect actions can cause reputational or financial damage. This report gauges how companies view the quality of the outputs produced by their analytics agents and explores how organizations are seeking to boost insight quality and get their agents working harder for the business. Some key findings from the report include the following: Agentic analytics is only just starting to deliver. On average, 48% of insights generated by analytics agents at the surveyed companies lead to actions that improve the business. That is a marked advance from the 37% average the respondents say generated such actions one year ago. But it means that more than half of the insights generated by analytics agents today are still failing to help businesses. Better quality of insights leads to clear business advantage. At a small cohort of organizations, which we term “insight leaders,” AI agents perform much better than the average. In this group, more than 70% of agent insights lead to actions that improve the business. The insight leaders also give the quality of their agents’ insights higher marks than do the total respondents overall. The quality gap is particularly wide when it comes to prescriptive insights. Insufficient context reduces insight quality. When analytics agents deliver insights of substandard quality, the main reason is a lack of business context, as cited by 55% of surveyed executives. Fragmented or inaccessible data is the other major factor, according to 45%. Fewer insight leaders say their agents struggle with access to context. Insight overload further inhibits agent effectiveness. At a majority (52%) of surveyed organizations, analytics agents generate too many insights to be properly evaluated and therefore acted upon. Less than one-quarter (24%) are able to evaluate all agent insights; most do so on a case-by-case basis, and that process is currently human-intensive. Governance and semantics are areas of focus for improving insights. The surveyed companies are prioritizing initiatives that enable better agent insights by strengthening AI and data governance (cited by 60%). They are also adding a semantic layer to their data architecture (45%). The experts we interviewed agree that the semantic layer is crucial to ensure high-performing agents. Download the report This content was produced by Insights, MIT Technology Review’s custom content arm, not its editorial staff. It was researched and written by humans, with any AI tools that may have been used limited to production processes under human oversight.

items.title: AIエージェント運用の始め方！本番で止まらない管理項目・体制・改善サイクルを解説
items.description: AIエージェントを本番に出したものの、誤った操作が起きたとき誰が何を見て止めるのか決まっていない。本記事では、 AIエージェントの運用で管理すべき7つの項目と、運用を始める5つのステップ を、運用設計書や稟議にそのまま使える形で解説します。 PoCではうまく動いたAIエージェントも、本番では誤回答や想定外のツール実行が起こります。従来のシステム監視だけでは判断の正しさを確かめられず、運用担当が不安を抱えたまま利用だけが広がりがちです。 Gartnerは、 2027年末までにエージェント型AIプロジェクトの40%超が中止される と予測しています。理由として挙げられているのは、コストの高騰、ビジネス価値の不明確さ、不十分なリスク管理です。運用の仕組みがないまま広げると、原因を追えずにプロジェクトごと止まる側に入るでしょう。 出典： Gartner Predicts Over 40% of Agentic AI Projects Will Be Canceled by End of 2027（Gartner） 本記事では、権限・承認・ログ・評価・コストといった運用の管理項目と、目的設定から定例レビューまでの運用ステップを中心に解説します。 読み終えれば、 自社の運用設計書のたたき台と、経営層に運用コストと効果を説明する材料 がそろいます。本番で止まらないAIエージェント運用の型を、順に確認していきましょう。 AIエージェントの運用が従来のシステム運用と異なる3つの点 AIエージェントの運用が従来のシステム運用と異なる点は、以下の3つです。 出力が確率的で同じ結果になるとは限らない 外部ツールを操作し業務に直接影響する モデルやプロンプトの更新で挙動が変わる 違いを押さえておくと、従来の監視項目のどこを足せばよいかが見えてきます。 出力が確率的で同じ結果になるとは限らない AIエージェントは、 同じ入力でも毎回同じ判断をするとは限りません 。 LLMは確率的に次の言葉を選ぶため、計画の立て方や呼び出すツールの順番が実行ごとに揺れます。従来のシステムのように「エラーが出ていなければ正常」とは判断できません。 たとえば社内問い合わせ対応のエージェントが、昨日は正しく答えた質問に対し、今日は改定前の規程を引用して回答するケースがあります。システム上はエラーではないため、死活監視では検知できません。 出力の品質を継続的に測る前提で運用を組めば、 利用者からの苦情が出る前に劣化へ気づけます 。 外部ツールを操作し業務に直接影響する AIエージェントは文章を返すだけでなく、 メール送信やデータ更新といった操作を自ら実行します 。 チャット型の生成AIなら、誤った回答は人が読んだ時点で止められます。一方でエージェントは、CRMの更新、チケットの起票、顧客へのメール送信までを人の確認なしに進められるため、誤りがそのまま業務に反映されます。 営業支援エージェントが宛先リストを取り違え、別の顧客に見積もりを送ってしまうと、取り消しはできません。影響は社内にとどまらず、取引先との信頼問題に発展します。 操作ごとに権限と承認の要否を決めておけば、 任せる範囲を広げても事故の影響を小さく抑えられます 。 モデルやプロンプトの更新で挙動が変わる AIエージェントは、 コードを変えなくても挙動が変わる 点も従来のシステムと異なります。 LLM提供元によるモデルの更新、プロンプトの修正、参照する社内文書の追加など、変更の入口が複数あります。どれか1つが変わるだけで、回答の傾向や呼び出すツールが変わります。 CIO Japanの解説では、ツールの追加、権限の変更、外部送信経路の追加、扱うデータ分類の拡大を、必ず再評価すべき変更として挙げています。モデル更新は影響が大きい場合に再評価し、小さな変更は回帰テストで吸収する考え方です。 出典： AIエージェント導入のガバナンス：社内規程・評価・監査を形にする方法（CIO Japan） 変更の種類ごとに再評価のルールを決めておくと、 改善のたびに品質が下がるリスクを避けられます 。 AIエージェントの運用で管理すべき7つの項目 AIエージェントの運用で管理すべき項目は、以下の7つです。 権限とアクセス範囲 人間の承認ポイント 実行ログとトレース 出力品質の評価 コストとトークン使用量 インシデント対応と停止手順 バージョンと変更管理 どれか1つが欠けると、事故の原因を追えなかったり、効果を説明できなかったりする穴になります。 権限とアクセス範囲 最初に管理すべきは、 エージェントが触れるデータと実行できる操作の範囲 です。 開発時に「とりあえず動かすため」に広い権限を付けたまま本番に出すと、誤作動やプロンプトインジェクションの被害が大きくなります。業務に必要な最小限の権限に絞ることが原則です。 具体的には、参照できるフォルダ、書き込みできるシステム、外部への送信可否をエージェントごとに一覧にします。共有の管理者アカウントではなく、エージェント専用のIDを発行すると、誰の操作かを後から区別できます。 権限一覧があれば、 セキュリティ部門のレビューや監査への説明がスムーズに進みます 。 人間の承認ポイント 人間の承認は、 取り消しが効かない操作に絞って挟む のが基本です。 すべての操作に承認を求めると、担当者が承認待ちの処理に追われ、エージェントを入れた意味がなくなります。逆に承認がまったくないと、誤った送金や一斉送信をその場で止められません。 判断の目安として、操作を以下の3段階に分けておくと設計しやすくなります。 自動実行してよい操作：社内文書の検索、下書きの作成など 承認が必要な操作：社外へのメール送信、支払い処理、データの削除など 禁止する操作：個人情報の外部送信、権限設定の変更など 段階を決めておくと、 運用実績に応じて自動実行の範囲を少しずつ広げられます 。 実行ログとトレース ログは会話履歴だけでは足りず、 判断の途中経過まで追えるトレース として残す必要があります。 トレースとは、1回のタスクの中でエージェントが何を参照し、どのツールをどの引数で呼び、どんな結果を得たかを順に記録したものです。最終出力だけでは、どの段階で判断を誤ったのかを特定できません。 CIO Japanの解説でも、参照したドキュメントの識別子、ツール呼び出しの履歴と引数、実行した権限、結果の成否、外部送信の有無を追えるようにすることが挙げられています。 出典： AIエージェント導入のガバナンス：社内規程・評価・監査を形にする方法（CIO Japan） トレースは後から追加しにくいため、 本番公開前の段階で記録の仕組みを組み込んでおきましょう 。 出力品質の評価 品質は感覚ではなく、 評価用データセットと基準を決めて定期的に測ります 。 「最近回答がおかしい気がする」という声だけでは、改善すべき箇所も、改善できたかどうかもわかりません。同じ問題セットで繰り返し測ることで、変化を比較できるようになります。 評価用データセットは、実際の問い合わせやタスクから代表的なものを数十件選び、正解や合格基準を付けて作ります。タスクを最後までやり遂げたか、手順は適切だったか、禁止操作をしていないかを採点項目にすると実務に沿います。 評価の仕組みがあれば、 モデルやプロンプトを変えるたびに品質への影響を数字で確認できます 。 コストとトークン使用量 AIエージェントのコストは、 1タスクあたりで見ないと実態をつかめません 。 エージェントは1つのタスクの中でLLMを何度も呼び出し、ツールの結果を読み込むたびにトークンを消費します。処理が行き詰まって同じ手順を繰り返すと、1件のタスクだけで想定の何倍もの費用がかかります。 月の請求額だけでなく、タスクごとのトークン消費とLLM呼び出し回数を記録しましょう。1タスクあたりの上限回数や月次の予算アラートを設定しておくと、暴走による急な請求を防げます。 1タスクあたりのコストがわかれば、 人が処理した場合の人件費と比べて投資対効果を説明できます 。 インシデント対応と停止手順 運用開始前に、 誰がどの手順でエージェントを止めるか を決めておきます。 誤った一斉送信や想定外のデータ更新が起きたとき、止め方が決まっていないと被害が広がり続けます。担当者を探しているあいだにも、エージェントは処理を進めてしまいます。 CIO Japanの解説では、封じ込めの手段として、キルスイッチ、トークンの失効、権限の剥奪、外部送信のブロックが挙げられています。あわせて、疑似インシデントの演習で「止められるか」「追えるか」を定期的に確認することも勧めています。 出典： AIエージェント導入のガバナンス：社内規程・評価・監査を形にする方法（CIO Japan） 停止手順が決まっていれば、 事故が起きても原因調査と再開判断まで落ち着いて進められます 。 バージョンと変更管理 AIエージェントでは、 プロンプト・モデル・ツール・参照データの組み合わせ をバージョンとして管理します。 コードだけを管理していても、プロンプトの1行の修正やモデルの切り替えで挙動は変わります。どの組み合わせで動いていたかがわからないと、品質が落ちたときに元へ戻せません。 変更のたびに、変更内容、変更者、評価結果、本番反映日を記録しておきましょう。担当者が異動しても、記録が残っていれば後任が経緯を追えます。 変更履歴をそろえておくと、 誰も中身を説明できない「野良エージェント」化を防げます 。 AIエージェントの運用を始める5つのステップ AIエージェントの運用は、以下の5つのステップで仕組みを整えます。 ステップ1：運用の目的と停止基準を決める ステップ2：運用体制と責任者を決める ステップ3：監視とログの仕組みを整える ステップ4：評価データで品質を測る ステップ5：定例レビューで改善を回す 順番どおりに進めると、本番公開後に「決めていなかった」で手が止まる場面を減らせます。 ステップ1：運用の目的と停止基準を決める 最初に、 エージェントに何を達成させるかと、どうなったら止めるか を文書にします。 目的があいまいなまま運用を始めると、何をもって成功とするかが決まらず、改善の優先順位も付けられません。停止基準がないと、問題が起きても「もう少し様子を見よう」と判断が先送りされます。 目的は「問い合わせの一次回答を自動化し、担当者の対応件数を減らす」のように業務の言葉で書きます。停止基準は「誤送信が1件でも起きたら即停止」「評価スコアが基準を2週連続で下回ったら利用範囲を縮小」のように具体的に決めましょう。 目的と停止基準があれば、 関係者のあいだで判断がぶれず、撤退か継続かも合理的に決められます 。 ステップ2：運用体制と責任者を決める 次に、 エージェントごとに責任者を1人決める ことから体制づくりを始めます。 AIエージェントは、モデル、プロンプト、ツール、データ、運用と関わる要素が多く、責任があいまいになりやすい仕組みです。誰の持ち物かが決まっていないと、問題が起きたときに部署間で押し付け合いが起きます。 責任者は業務部門から立て、監視担当、セキュリティ確認、変更承認の窓口をあわせて決めます。役割の詳細は、後述の「AIエージェントの運用体制と役割分担」で解説します。 責任者が明確なら、 現場からの要望や不具合報告がたらい回しにならず、改善の速度が上がります 。 ステップ3：監視とログの仕組みを整える 体制が決まったら、 トレースとアラートを本番公開前に設定 します。 監視の仕組みがないまま公開すると、問題は利用者からの苦情で初めて発覚します。その時点では原因を追うためのログが残っておらず、再発防止策も立てられません。 設定しておきたい監視項目は以下のとおりです。 タスクごとのトレース：参照データ、ツール呼び出し、結果の記録 エラーとタイムアウト：ツール呼び出しの失敗や処理の中断 コストのアラート：1タスクの呼び出し回数や月次予算の超過 禁止操作の検知：承認なしの外部送信や権限外アクセスの試行 監視ツールは、後述の「AIエージェントの運用を支える監視・評価ツール」から構築環境に合うものを選ぶと、 自前で仕組みを作る手間を省けます 。 ステップ4：評価データで品質を測る 監視と並行して、 評価用データセットで品質の基準値を取ります 。 基準値がなければ、運用中に品質が上がったのか下がったのかを判断できません。公開時点のスコアを記録しておくことで、以後の変更の良し悪しを比べられます。 評価は、人が採点する方法と、LLMに採点させる方法を組み合わせるのが現実的です。全件を人が見るのは負担が大きいため、LLMで一次採点し、低スコアや判定が割れたものだけを人が確認します。 本番で失敗したタスクを評価データに追加していけば、 同じ失敗を繰り返さないための回帰テストとして機能します 。 ステップ5：定例レビューで改善を回す 最後に、 月次の定例レビュー で運用状況を確認し、改善を決める場を作ります。 ログと評価結果が集まっても、見る場がなければ改善にはつながりません。担当者が日々の対応に追われ、気づいた問題が放置されるのはよくあるパターンです。 レビューでは、KPIの推移、発生したインシデント、失敗タスクの傾向、現場からの要望を確認します。そのうえで、プロンプトの修正、権限の見直し、自動実行範囲の拡大や縮小を決め、次回のレビューで効果を確かめます。 改善の記録が積み上がると、 経営層への報告や次のエージェント導入の判断材料 としても使えます。 AIエージェントの運用体制と役割分担 AIエージェントの運用体制は、以下の4つの役割で分担します。 業務オーナー 運用担当 情シス・セキュリティ部門 法務・リスク管理部門 「決める人」「作る人」「見張る人」を分けておくと、1人の担当者に負荷と判断が集中しません。 業務オーナーが担う役割 業務オーナーは、 エージェントの目的と利用範囲を決める最終責任者 です。 エージェントが成果を出しているかどうかは、業務を理解している人でなければ判断できません。情シスやDX推進部門が持ち主になると、技術的には動いていても業務の役に立っていない状態に気づけません。 業務オーナーは、目的と停止基準の決定、自

items.title: AIエージェントのカスタマーサポート活用術！できることと導入事例
items.description: 問い合わせは増え続けるのにオペレーターは採用できず、FAQチャットボットを入れても結局有人対応に回ってくる。本記事では、 カスタマーサポートでAIエージェントに任せられる業務と、Klarna・KDDI・東京海上日動などの公式発表に基づく導入事例 を中心に解説します。 応答待ち時間の長期化や対応品質のばらつきに悩みながら、新しい打ち手を探しているCS部門の責任者は多いでしょう。シナリオ型のチャットボットでは想定外の質問に答えられず、期待した削減効果が出ないケースも少なくありません。 AIエージェントは、問い合わせの意図を読み取り、返金や契約変更などの手続きまで自律的に進められる点がチャットボットと異なります。仕組みを理解しないまま製品を選ぶと、チャットボットの二の舞で費用だけがかかるでしょう。 本記事では、AIエージェントがカスタマーサポートでできること、企業の導入事例、製品の選び方と導入手順を整理しています。 読み終えれば、 AIに任せる業務と人が担う業務の線引き ができ、社内稟議に使える導入イメージを描けるようになります。 カスタマーサポートにおけるAIエージェントとは？チャットボットとの違い カスタマーサポートにおけるAIエージェントとは、顧客の問い合わせ意図を理解し、回答だけでなく手続きの実行まで自律的に進めるAIです。役割の違いは以下の3つで整理できます。 AIエージェントは問い合わせの解決まで自律的に実行する 従来型チャットボットはシナリオどおりに回答する 有人オペレーターとAIエージェントは役割を分担する 違いを押さえておくと、既存のチャットボットで解決できなかった課題をどこまで任せられるか判断しやすくなります。 AIエージェントは問い合わせの解決まで自律的に実行する AIエージェントの最大の特徴は、 回答で終わらず、問い合わせの解決まで自ら進める 点です。 大規模言語モデル（LLM）が問い合わせの意図を読み取り、必要な情報を社内ナレッジやCRMから探して、次に取るべき行動を判断します。 たとえば「注文した商品の配送先を変えたい」という問い合わせであれば、本人確認、注文情報の照会、配送先の変更処理、完了の通知までを一連の流れで実行します。 顧客は担当者の折り返しを待たずに用件を済ませられるため、 問い合わせ1件あたりの解決時間を大きく縮められます 。 従来型チャットボットはシナリオどおりに回答する 従来型チャットボットは、 あらかじめ設計したシナリオやFAQの範囲でしか回答できません 。 質問文をキーワードや選択肢で判定し、登録済みの回答を返す仕組みのためです。想定外の言い回しや、複数の用件が混ざった質問には対応しきれません。 2つの違いは以下のとおりです。 比較項目 AIエージェント 従来型チャットボット 回答の作り方 意図を読み取り、ナレッジから回答を生成する シナリオやFAQの登録回答を返す 対応範囲 手続きの実行まで担う 情報提供が中心 運用負荷 ナレッジの整備が中心 シナリオの作成と更新が必要 シナリオ更新に追われている現場ほど、AIエージェントへの移行で運用負荷を下げられます。 有人オペレーターとAIエージェントは役割を分担する AIエージェントを導入しても、 オペレーターが不要になるわけではありません 。 クレーム対応や個別事情の判断など、感情への配慮や例外処理が必要な問い合わせは、人が対応したほうが顧客満足度を保てるためです。 現実的な分担は、定型的な問い合わせをAIエージェントが完結させ、判断が難しいものは会話履歴ごとオペレーターに引き継ぐ形です。オペレーター側でも、AIが提示する回答案を使って応対を速められます。 分担を先に決めておくと、 導入後に「AIに任せすぎて顧客が離れる」事態を防げます 。 AIエージェントがカスタマーサポートでできること5つ AIエージェントがカスタマーサポートでできることは以下の5つです。 一次回答を24時間自動で返す 注文変更や返金などの手続きを完結させる 電話の問い合わせに音声で応対する オペレーターに回答案とナレッジを提示する 応対履歴から顧客の声を分析する 自社の問い合わせのうち、どれに当てはまる業務が多いかを確認しながら読み進めてください。 一次回答を24時間自動で返す AIエージェントは、 営業時間外や繁忙期でも問い合わせに即時回答 できます。 人員配置に左右されないため、夜間や休日、キャンペーン直後の問い合わせ集中時でも待ち時間が発生しません。 ログイン方法、料金プランの違い、解約手順など、マニュアルやFAQに答えがある質問は、AIエージェントが社内ナレッジを参照して回答を組み立てます。質問の言い回しが登録済みのFAQと違っていても、意図が同じであれば回答できます。 よくある質問を自己解決してもらえると、 オペレーターの受電件数そのものを減らせます 。 注文変更や返金などの手続きを完結させる AIエージェントは、 基幹システムやCRMと連携して手続きまで完結 させられます。 API経由で注文管理や会員管理のシステムを操作できるためです。回答だけのチャットボットでは、手続きの段階で有人対応に切り替える必要がありました。 具体的には以下のような手続きを任せられます。 注文内容や配送先の変更 返品・返金の受付 契約プランの変更や登録情報の更新 手続き系の問い合わせは件数が多いため、ここを自動化できると削減効果が大きくなります。 電話の問い合わせに音声で応対する チャットだけでなく、 電話の問い合わせにも音声で応対するAIエージェント が登場しています。 音声認識と音声合成の精度が上がり、IVR（自動音声応答）のように番号を押させるのではなく、顧客の話し言葉をそのまま理解して会話できるようになったためです。 国内でも、neoAIが本人確認や契約変更を含めた顧客対応を音声で担うボイスエージェントを2026年10月に正式提供しています。 高齢の顧客が多く電話窓口を閉じられない業界でも、 電話のまま自動化を進められる 選択肢になります。 オペレーターに回答案とナレッジを提示する AIエージェントは顧客対応だけでなく、 応対中のオペレーターを裏側から支援 する役割も担えます。 通話やチャットの内容をリアルタイムで読み取り、該当するマニュアルや過去の回答例を探して、回答案として画面に表示します。オペレーターは保留にして資料を探す手間を省けます。 東京海上日動のコンタクトセンターでも、通話をテキスト化して回答案をオペレーターに提示する仕組みが2026年3月から稼働しています。 経験の浅いオペレーターでもベテランに近い回答ができるため、 新人の育成期間を短くできます 。 応対履歴から顧客の声を分析する AIエージェントは、 蓄積された応対履歴をもとに顧客の声（VoC）を分析 できます。 これまで担当者が手作業で分類していた問い合わせ内容を、AIが自動で要約・分類するためです。件数の多い不満や、急に増えた問い合わせの傾向をすばやく把握できます。 たとえば「アプリ更新後にログインできない」という問い合わせが急増していれば、開発部門へ早期に共有できます。製品改善やFAQの追加につなげれば、問い合わせの発生自体を減らせます。 サポート部門が「問い合わせを処理する部署」から 「顧客の声を事業に還元する部署」 へ役割を広げられます。 AIエージェントをカスタマーサポートに導入するメリット AIエージェントをカスタマーサポートに導入するメリットは以下の3つです。 応答待ち時間を短縮できる オペレーターが複雑な対応に集中できる 応対品質のばらつきを抑えられる 稟議で導入効果を説明するときの論点としても使えます。 応答待ち時間を短縮できる 最もわかりやすいメリットは、 顧客の待ち時間を短縮できる ことです。 AIエージェントは同時に多数の問い合わせを処理できるため、電話がつながらない、チャットの順番待ちが続くといった状況が起きにくくなります。 Klarnaは、AIアシスタントの導入により問い合わせの解決時間が約11分から2分未満に短縮されたと公表しています。 待ち時間は顧客満足度に直結するため、 解約やSNSでの不満投稿を減らす効果 も期待できます。 オペレーターが複雑な対応に集中できる 定型的な問い合わせをAIエージェントに任せると、 オペレーターは人にしかできない対応に時間を使えます 。 パスワード再設定のような単純な問い合わせに追われる状態では、丁寧な説明が必要な相談やクレームに十分な時間を割けません。 AIが一次対応を担えば、オペレーターは解約を考えている顧客への引き止めや、高額商品の購入相談など、売上や継続率に影響する対応に注力できます。 単純作業が減ると業務のやりがいも高まり、 オペレーターの離職を抑える 効果にもつながります。 応対品質のばらつきを抑えられる AIエージェントは、 同じナレッジにもとづいて一定の品質で回答 します。 人による対応では、経験年数や知識量によって回答の正確さや言葉づかいに差が出ます。担当者によって説明が違うと、顧客の不信感につながりかねません。 AIエージェントが参照するナレッジを一元管理しておけば、制度変更や新商品の情報も更新した時点で全応対に反映されます。オペレーター支援で使えば、人の回答品質もそろえられます。 品質が安定すると、 SVによる応対チェックや指導の工数 も減らせます。 カスタマーサポートにAIエージェントを導入した企業の事例 カスタマーサポートにAIエージェントを導入した企業の事例を、各社の公式発表をもとに4つ紹介します。 Klarnaはチャット対応の3分の2をAIに任せた KDDIはau PAYの問い合わせにAIエージェントを導入した 東京海上日動はオペレーターの応対をAIで支援している ベルシステム24は複雑な問い合わせに答えるAIを開発した 顧客対応の自動化とオペレーター支援の両方の事例があるため、自社に近い形を探してみてください。 Klarnaはチャット対応の3分の2をAIに任せた スウェーデンの決済企業Klarna（クラーナ）は、 導入1か月でカスタマーサービスのチャットの3分の2をAIアシスタントが処理した と2024年2月に発表しました。 OpenAIの技術を使ったAIアシスタントで、返金、返品、支払いに関する問い合わせなどに35以上の言語で対応しています。 同社の発表による成果は以下のとおりです。 最初の1か月で230万件の会話を処理し、フルタイム担当者700人分の業務量に相当 顧客満足度は人による対応と同等 再問い合わせが25%減少 顧客は希望すれば人と話すこともできる設計です。 AIと有人対応の選択肢を残したまま自動化を進めた 点は、導入時の参考になります。 > Klarnaの発表はこちらから KDDIはau PAYの問い合わせにAIエージェントを導入した KDDIは、 お客さまセンターの応対実績をもとに独自開発したAIエージェント を、2026年3月から問い合わせ対応に導入しています。 KDDI総合研究所と開発したもので、人の応対を学習して再現し、回答の根拠を自ら確認する仕組みを備えています。2025年11月の発表時点で、回答精度は約90%、1人あたりの応対時間は約70%削減を見込むとしています。 導入先は「auサポート AIアドバイザー」と「チャットサポート」です。まずau PAY、au PAY カード、Pontaポイントの問い合わせから始め、2026年度内をめどにauサービス全体へ広げる計画です。 対象サービスを絞って始め、段階的に広げる 進め方は、大規模な窓口を持つ企業の参考になります。 > KDDI総合研究所の発表はこちらから 東京海上日動はオペレーターの応対をAIで支援している 東京海上日動は、 コンタクトセンターの主要業務にAIを活用した業務支援基盤 items.title: Additional Course Context (for AI Safety Fundamentals; unofficial)
items.description: Context: I created this to share before the start of courses I facilitate to provide a bunch of additional context and frames. I emphasise to students that these posts are to be considered as bonus content —not core curriculum content—and that as such they are really just there for students who want to go deeper, before or after the course. I also provide a lot of links; this is to make it easy for students to follow up anything that catches their interest. Some general thoughts on advice I suspect that most advice (including most of the advice I’ve given in the past) is bad. People have very different goals, personalities, skills and opportunities and unless you know someone them really well, it’s hard to cater advice to their circumstances. What one person needs to hear, may be the absolute worst thing for another. In traditional societies with a slow rate of change, elders are revered. What you’re going through, they’ve lived through and so learning from their experience can save you vast amounts of pain. However, modern Western societies are marked by a much more rapid rate of change and so the experience of elder’s isn’t valued to the same degree. For better or worse, people tend to be much more skeptical that what worked then will still work now. I view the rapid pace of AI progress as greatly exacerbating these kinds of epistemic challenges. I think it’s quite sensible to question how much anyone actually knows about the world we’re going into (I’m referring to both the world in general and AI safety/governance which are constantly shifting fields). Uncertainty is scary, but I see it as a fact of life, one we ultimately need to accept (counterpoint: how often does this end up becoming a form of defeatism?). Scott Alexander takes this skepticism of advice even further. Rather than just questioning how much we can trust advice, he provocatively suggests that you may want to reverse any advise you hear . People tend choose which groups to join based on whether they resonate with that group’s worldview. Scott suggests that it is often the people who wouldn’t join that group that most need to hear that group’s perspective and that the people who do join such groups who need to listen to the outside world. Unfortunately, groups are very good at taking individuals, solidifying their natural tendencies solidified into an ideology and then amplifying them to an extreme. During this course, you’ll be exposed to many reasons why you should worry more about AI. And perhaps most people should worry more about AI, but perhaps you, personally, are one of the people who should worry less. (See also Zizek’s criticism of wisdom : “Whatever you do, a wise man will come and justify it”) Some thoughts on frameworks People often teach strategy by teaching you frameworks. We’ll be covering a few. I would argue that every framework has strengths and weaknesses; and that every framework is dependent on certain underlying assumptions. Not knowing the assumptions or limitations of a framework doesn’t mean they don’t exist; it just means that you don’t know them. The last few sentences describe a meta-framework. This meta-framework has weaknesses and assumptions as well. Were you nodding along to the previous few lines? If so, do you know the weaknesses and assumptions of the meta-framework I just described. If you didn’t know these, did you know that you didn’t know, or are these an unknown unknown? Even if a framework is “correct” in some objective sense—humans being humans—it’s still possible that using the framework will on average make your decisions worse. For example, take consistency. Being inconsistent is generally agreed to be objectively wrong, but it’s quite easy to imagine scenarios where someone talks themselves into making a mind-blowingly stupid decision because “I had to be consistent” (with past decisions they couldn’t psychologically admit were mistaken). Frustratingly, it’s also very common for someone to use a framework that is more or less fake to make decisions that are better on net than the decisions they would have otherwise made. This is quite unfair, but the universe doesn’t have to play nice . Unfortunately, strategy is hard. Steven Schubert writes : “I think it may be a bit underrated how valuable analysis from the very best analysts of the future of AI is, relative to that of pretty good analysts. It’s such a complex issue it’s easy to miss vital considerations. It pushes the limit of human intellectual ability.” Cruxes when attempting to predict the future: Default beliefs and burden of proof: Do we take claims about transformative AI as highly unusual claims that must satisfy a strong burden of proof, or do we treat these as relatively normal claims on the basis that we already have invented several technologies that would have been almost beyond belief for our ancestors? Is the burden of proof on those who would regulate a technology (ie. a default presumption that regulation is harmful) or on those who want to build it (ie. the company needs to prove their product is safe)? Evidence provided by conceptual arguments: Do we treat these as essentially trustworthy if written with a sufficient degree of care and evaluated by folks with good judgement or do we treat them as groundless speculation, at least relative to the null hypothesis or arguments that rely more heavily on empirical results? Can we project exponential trends into the future on the basis of induction (ie. the future being like the past) or is this foolish given that exponentials must end at some point? Development of many technologies has occurred as a series of s-curves (ie. sigmoids) which would support the latter view, in contrast, Astralcodex points out that simply knowing that something is a sigmoid doesn’t tell you where you are on the curve (a hilarious graph from the World Energy Organisation shows them repeatedly, incorrectly predicting that exponential progress in terms of solar power will finish. items.title: Import AI 479: Spacewar; low-latency tasks versus LLMs; Genie 4
items.description: Welcome to Import AI, a newsletter about AI research. Import AI runs on arXiv, cappuccinos, and feedback from readers. If you’d like to support this, please subscribe. Subscribe now LLMs are very bad at low-latency tasks: …Realtime-Bench says it’ll be a while till AI systems can play games or do online auctions for you… Researchers have built Realtime-Bench, “a suite of carefully curated dynamic tasks where delayed actions directly affect success”. The test helps evaluate how well modern, general-purpose AI systems can perform tasks where decisions need to be made in real-time. The benchmark consists of 50 interactive game and web tasks, split across 30 web tasks in four categories (travel, e-commerce, service, and security), and 20 game tasks (arcade, puzzle, strategy, and simulation). Who did the research: The benchmark was built by people at the University of Texas at Austin, Ohio State University, University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign, NVIDIA, Northwestern University, and Steadyworks. What it measures: The test is designed to probe for three qualities: temporal state awareness (”RT-Perceive”), where models can use observations to track changes in the world; adaptive deliberation (”RT-Deliberate”), where models alter their reasoning length and depth according to available time; and time-aware action selection (”RT-Act”) where models need to appropriately time their actions for the situation. “For example, an agent purchasing a ticket must track the sale status and assess whether observed availability is still current (RT-Perceive), limit further deliberation when the purchase window is closing (RT-Deliberate), and choose between waiting for sales to open and purchasing while tickets remain available (RT-Act).” They have three different conditions: Wall clock, which is designed to test out performance under real-world latency. Paused clock, which lets you arbitrarily pause things so you can get a sense of baseline capability, and Token clock, which “advances the environment at a fixed rate per generation token. An action is applied at the simulated time reached when it is committed, so consuming more tokens delays execution regardless of actual inference latency”. How well do models do? The authors tested out models from OpenAI (GPT-6-Astra, GPT-5.6 Sol, GPT-Realtime-2, OpenAI Decisions), Anthropic (Claude Fable 5.1, Claude Opus 5), Google (Gemini 3.8 Flash, Gemini 3.1 Flash Live, Gemini 3.8 Live), Jev 1.13, as well as Chinese models from Deepseek (V4.1) and Moonshot AI (Kimi-K3). GPT-6 Astra (high) got the highest pass rate on the ‘wall clock’ evaluation setting, with 36%. By comparison, with a paused clock, models with high reasoning get closer to 70% or even 80% success. Why this matters: This benchmark is an effective proxy for where AI agents will break – the low scores here point to tasks where AI agents cannot yet be expected to perform well. Check out the leaderboard : Realtime-Bench (official website) . Read the paper : Realtime-Bench: Can Frontier Models Solve Real-time Interactive Problems? (arXiv) . *** The future of spacewar, courtesy of the Defense Intelligence Agency: …Anti-satellite tech, space nukes, and more… Working in AI can be stressful so sometimes to relax myself I like to read about other topics to get a sense for what horrors lie elsewhere. I take the same approach with depression, where if I feel sad I will try and listen to music by people sadder than me in an attempt to cheer myself up (e.g., Radiohead, Neil Young, and in very dark moments Bill Callahan / Smog, etc). So with that in mind I recently read “Challenges to Security in Space”, by the Defense Intelligence Agency. What’s going on in space: As with conflict on Earth, space is defined by conflict between the US versus China, Russia, Iran, and North Korea, with China the most technologically sophisticated, and Russia the most seemingly gung ho. “China and Russia are developing a formidable spectrum of offensive capabilities to degrade or destroy space services of other countries, from kinetic destruction to sophisticated jamming and cyber operations,” the DIA writes. “China has more than tripled its space launches per year in the past decade, with 22 launches in 2016 and 93 launches in 2025… Beijing judges space is central to the United States and its allies’ operations. Beijing also considers space an offensive military domain, which has shaped integral components of PLA military planning and campaigns.” Spacewar: The general vibe you get from reading this 100+ page report is there is a huge amount of ugly, frightening stuff happening in space, or being done to things in space by things on the ground. Some example quotes: “By the late 2020s, China may field space-based directed energy systems and higher-powered ground-based directed energy systems capable of threatening satellites in higher orbits” “China is developing space-based technology, including on-orbit counterspace weapons, capable of holding space systems at risk” “Russia’s Peresvet, a ground-based laser system, is designed to dazzle enemy satellites’ optical systems to mask the movement of Russia’s strategic missile systems” “Russia has launched several satellites over the last few years which conducted test activities on orbit for technologies that could enable attacks on other countries’ satellites and result in temporary or permanent damage” China has a couple of spaceplanes, akin to the US’s hyper-secret X-37B vehicle, and they appear to be getting more sophisticated. In 2023, one of China’s aforementioned vehicles, “released and interacted with an object.” Satellite-on-satellite fights: It’s obvious throughout the report that we’re in a world where rival nations have satellites that try to go up and mess with other satellites from other people. “In 2019, Russia launched satellite Cosmos 2542, which released a second satellite, Cosmos 2543. items.title: Some “coherence arguments” are two different things in a trenchcoat
items.description: The “two kids in a trenchcoat” trope , in case you haven’t heard of it. Image sources: 1 , 2 tl;dr I go through three “coherence arguments”, related to (1) market competition, (2) AI self-reflection and self-modification, and (3) AI training algorithms. I argue that each of these implies a pressure for (something like) “being self-consistent”, and also a pressure for (something like) “only caring about long-term eventual outcomes, with ruthless indifference to anything else”. But the latter pressure tends to be weaker and/or more contingent than the former. So it's bad to lump them together and call them by the same name. 1. An example “coherence argument” that I’ll focus on for most of the post I’ll talk about two other “coherence arguments” at the end (§6), but let’s start with the one based on market competition: In a stock market, people with circular preferences will systematically transfer money to those without circular preferences. For example, if I think I’m winning every time I trade A for B, and B for C, and C for A, then someone can just siphon off as much money as they like from me by repeatedly offering me deals that each look good to me in isolation, but in aggregate comprise a Dutch book against me. Now, that’s the case of circular preferences, but the core idea here goes well beyond just that. More broadly, over time, more and more of the wealth will wind up in the hands of those whose behavior is “coherent” (in some sense), and less and less of the wealth in the hands of those whose behavior is not. So over time, the market should be dominated by the former, not the latter, other things equal. And so when we look at the market later on, we’ll mostly be seeing self-consistent goal-directed behavior. 2. My headline claim Everything in those paragraphs above is technically correct (“the best kind of correct”), but I will argue that it’s often taken to encompass two different phenomena wearing a trenchcoat. In one of them, people wind up with a smaller fraction of the wealth on purpose : they’re forgoing some wealth in exchange for something else that they wanted more. In the other, people wind up with a smaller fraction of the wealth by accident . The argument above applies equally to both: the argument only cares about people’s behavior, not their motivations. (Indeed, the argument would apply equally well to a market of mindless trading algorithms that have no motivations at all.) But the two phenomena tend to play out in very different ways—in particular, one is generally a much stronger effect than the other. Indeed, for all three “coherence arguments” in this post (§1 above, plus two more in §6 below), we wind up with (loosely speaking): a strong pressure for (something like) “doing well by your own lights”, or “acting like you have self-consistent desires”, a weak or contingent pressure for those desires to be more specifically long-term “goal-directed” / “consequentialist”—i.e., concerning what outcomes will ultimately happen in the future …as opposed to, say, “a desire to always act with integrity in the moment”, or even “a myopic desire to spin around in circles right now”. Thus these “coherence arguments” are not wrong , but they are pedagogically dicey —a recipe for confusion, especially via accidental conflation of the strong effect with the weak effect. (And in the AI risk context, it’s the weak effect that matters for ruthless power-seeking, incorrigibility, and all the other aspects of instrumental convergence.) We should stop talking like that. Instead, we should take the trenchcoat off and talk about its two component phenomena separately, and refer to them by different names. Game-plan for the rest of the post: I will go through the two component phenomena in §4, and then why it’s so hazardous to lump them together in §5, and finally zip through two more “coherence arguments” in §6 and why they suffer from this same issue. …But first, if anyone cares, how did I come to write this post? 3. (Backstory of this post) I just had a long argument with @habryka about whether the title of @Rohin Shah ’s “Coherence arguments do not entail goal-directed behavior” (2018) is good (my position) or bad (his position). Alas, I kept misunderstanding Habryka until he quit in frustration before we resolved it. But I think I finally get where he’s coming from? I think his position is something like (my words): For example, take that market competition argument in §1 above. It’s “a coherence argument”. And it “entails goal-directed behavior”. So obviously, the sentence “Coherence arguments do not entail goal-directed behavior” is misleading. Why on earth are you being so dense? That’s fair! I was indeed being dense! (And for the record, I concede on the question of Rohin’s title.) Why was I being dense? Because it’s a position grounded in a conceptual framework where we’re OK with lumping the two things together under one trenchcoat, [1] and my brain was so opposed to that framing, that it refused to even entertain it as a possibility—even while Habryka kept repeating it in increasingly clear and exasperated ways. More broadly, I’ve felt for years like there’s something amiss in how certain people (especially @Eliezer Yudkowsky and Habryka) think and talk about “coherence”. But I’ve failed to pin down exactly what it was. Maybe this is part of it? (Either way, many thanks to Habryka for his time and energy.) 4. Then at the end of the day, whoops, where did all my money go? This phenomenon is important, and the term “coherence” is obviously appropriate for describing it. items.title: The U.S. Census Bureau and “Super Intelligence”
items.description: I was reminded today of AI Adoption Rate Trending Down for Large Companies , a chart produced by Apollo Global Management in September 2025, which appeared to show a slowdown in U.S. corporate AI adoption based on numbers collected by the U.S. Census Bureau. At the time I used that chart to demonstrate GPT-5 data analysis , and then to experiment with Claude's new Code Interpreter . I decided to try running those numbers again to see what had changed over the past year, and in doing so learned that the Bureau has fallen foul of Executive Order 14434 , aka the asinine Super Intelligence one. First, the updated chart Every two weeks the U.S. Census Bureau runs a survey called the Business Trends and Outlook Survey (aka BTOS). Each time it goes to 200,000 businesses out of 1.2 million total - the surveyed group (a "panel") cycles such that an individual business only completes the survey every twelve weeks. The latest data is published on alternating Thursdays at 10am. I used the most recent numbers (published October 22, 2026) to create a new version ( GPT-6 Astra Extra High transcript ) of the AI adoption chart, updated to reflect both the last twelve months and a change that was made to the survey question sent out by the Bureau: For comparison, here's that AI adoption chart from last year (my GPT-5 version): In September 2025 the largest (250+ employees) companies answered "yes" around 12% of the time to the question about whether they used AI in "producing goods or services". Under the new "any business function" wording, by February 2026, those same large companies answered "yes" around 30% of the time, and by October 2026 that had increased to around 40%. The data in the above chart comes from the "Employment size class" XLSX file, available from here . Here's a copy of the file I used. You can view the survey document that is sent out to businesses - here's my snapshot copy of that 346KB PDF. The changing language of the questions As the chart demonstrates, the question asked by the Bureau changed in a material way on November 17th, 2025. Prior to that date, the question they asked was this (emphasis mine): In the last two weeks, did this business use Artificial Intelligence (AI) in producing goods or services ? (Examples of AI: machine learning, natural language processing, virtual agents, voice recognition, etc.) On December 3rd, 2025, the Bureau announced a significant change to that question. Here's the replacement: In the last two weeks, did this business use Artificial Intelligence (AI) in any of its business functions ? (Examples of AI: machine learning, natural language processing, virtual agents, voice recognition, etc.) No more "producing goods or services" - now it's "in any of its business functions"! This means that the answers to the question before and after November 17th are not directly comparable. From October 19, 2026, they ask about Super Intelligence When I went looking for the updated question language in the latest XLSX file, I couldn't find it. I found this instead: In the last two weeks, did this business use Super Intelligence or SI (formerly referred to as Artificial Intelligence or AI) in any of its business functions? (Examples of SI use include: SI-powered data analysis; generative SI for marketing, product design, or coding; virtual SI agents for customer service; SI-powered forecasting or pricing; SI-driven computer vision for quality control, etc.) The BTOS about page explains what happened: Beginning with the October 19, 2026 collection, instrument wording was updated due to Executive Order 14434 . The current numbers reflect the old Artificial Intelligence survey wording - the first survey results reflecting the Super Intelligence wording are due for publication on Thursday. Is this going to affect the survey? The obvious open question here is whether this wording change is going to affect the survey results. The businesses answering this survey will have last seen that question twelve weeks ago, when it was still called AI. Hopefully the new language isn't going to confuse them, especially since the survey helpfully spells out "formerly referred to as Artificial Intelligence or AI". I can't help but laugh at the absurdity of "SI-powered data analysis; generative SI for marketing, product design, or coding; virtual SI agents for customer service" though. items.title: Stop counting tokens, start counting what ships
items.description: When a developer gives an AI agent a coding task, the agent does more than answer once. It plans, generates code, runs tests, and repeats the process to correct errors. A single task can use 10 to 50 times more tokens than a basic chat prompt. The more useful the agent becomes, the more calls it makes. With per-token pricing, the workflows creating the most value can also become the most expensive. The financial pressure is already visible. Uber reportedly exhausted its entire 2026 AI budget by April after expanding its use of Claude Code. GitHub Copilot moved from flat-rate pricing to metered credits. Gartner predicts that AI coding token costs will surpass average developer salaries by 2028. The natural response is rationing usage caps, seat limits, and approvals before developers launch agents. But blanket limits can restrict the workflows delivering value. They also optimize the wrong number. Cost per token measures consumption, not results. Some spending reflects waste, including retries and runaway loops. Some represents the work of shipping software. A meter cannot distinguish them, and neither can a spending cap. Measure the software that ships A better measure is cost per merged pull request: total AI-assisted development cost divided by the number of changes that pass review and are merged. Track rework and defects alongside it so cheaper changes do not conceal lower quality. If that cost falls as AI usage rises, without compromising quality, developers are converting more consumption into useful software. The question is not how many tokens they use, but how much finished work the investment produces. Improving that equation requires two changes: reserve expensive inference for tasks that need it, and lower the cost of routine work. Match the model to the task Agentic coding does not require the most powerful model at every step. Use a frontier model, or an on-premises flagship when policy requires it, for difficult planning and novel reasoning. Route suitable work, including code generation, test creation, and repeated refactoring, to open-weight models you operate yourself. A gateway can route requests according to task complexity, data sensitivity, cost, and latency. This reserves premium inference for the moments that justify it rather than applying premium pricing to an entire workflow. Meter the exception, not the workload. Open-weight models make this division increasingly practical. Software-engineering benchmarks show that leading open-weight models can approach frontier performance on some tasks. That does not establish equivalence across every repository or workflow. Evaluate candidates against your own code, tests, and acceptance criteria before assigning production work. Change the economics of repeated use Next, decide who owns the capacity. With rented inference, every call adds to the bill. With owned capacity, most of the cost is committed upfront, so each additional call gets cheaper as usage grows. The economics are simple: per-token pricing makes heavy use more expensive, while owned capacity becomes more efficient as teams use it more. Ownership is not free, though. Power, operations, maintenance, and depreciation all must be considered. The number that matters is the fully loaded cost per merged pull request. Owned capacity also delivers a type of value that never appears on an invoice: control over sensitive code. When code generation and testing run on-premises, proprietary code stays inside the enterprise. Only approved planning prompts and governed exceptions go to external models, through a gateway the organization controls. That opens the sensitive repositories where security usually stalls adoption, and where the biggest gains are waiting. Test the operating model At HPE, a hybrid AI platform routes routine workloads from more than 150 internal applications to open-weight models running on premises, including on HPE Private Cloud AI. The result: token costs down 30 to 50%. That is the point of hybrid. With HPE Private Cloud AI, owning your inference does not mean giving up frontier models. Run the volume on capacity you own and let a gateway send the hardest work. Data also shows that usage, not licensed headcount, drives spend. The top 5% of users generated most of the consumption, and the heaviest used roughly 450 times more than the lightest on the same license. If power users grow from a small minority to half the workforce, monthly spend can rise about 4.4 times with flat headcount. Your mix will differ, which is exactly why you need to measure it. HPE tracks two metrics and recommends customers do the same. First, it tracks cost per active developer, because averaging across all licenses hides the power users driving spend. Second, it tracks cost per merged pull request, because it connects AI spending to software that ships. Baseline both costs before changing infrastructure. Then run a complete development cycle on owned capacity. If both metrics do not improve as usage grows, your current model may still be the better choice. Build for adoption, not rationing Owned capacity is not for everyone. Low or unpredictable usage favors APIs, with no capital tied up in idle infrastructure. Ownership pays off when sustained demand keeps it busy. Most enterprises will run hybrid: frontier APIs for demanding or intermittent work, owned capacity for repeatable volume. A governed gateway decides what leaves the building, so you get frontier models without giving up sovereignty over your code. As developers lean harder on coding agents, usage will keep rising. The real choice is whether that growth shows up as a bigger variable-cost bill or as more software shipped on capacity you own. The companies that lead AI-assisted development will not ration adoption to control costs. They will build an operating model where more AI use improves the economics instead of undermining them. items.title: The agentic web is here
items.description: In 2001, a decade after he invented the World Wide Web, Tim Berners-Lee articulated a new vision. Together with two colleagues, he published an article in the magazine Scientific American in which he outlined what he called the “Semantic Web” : an internet designed to be navigated by autonomous software agents that could address our every need, without requiring us to muck about with browsers and search engines ourselves. To illustrate what this might look like, Berners-Lee and his colleagues told a story about a pair of siblings who use their agents to automatically research and book physical therapy appointments for their mother, making sure they would be covered by insurance and fit their busy calendars. At the turn of the millennium, this vision seemed far-fetched: Google had only been online for a couple of years, and most people were still on dial-up connections. But a quarter-century on, the dream of autonomous software agents that use the internet and carry out tasks for us has finally been realized. New tools such as Meta’s blockbuster Muse agent, OpenAI’s Dots, and Anthropic’s Claude Duet are being given access to people’s email inboxes and bank accounts, Meanwhile, in a series of worrying incidents, agents created by OpenAI broke free of their sandboxes and caused havoc online. Just as the rise of smartphones sparked the development of a more atomized and attention-grabbing internet, the advent of powerful AI systems heralds a new era: We’re facing not the semantic web but the agentic web. This new web is developing out of sight and in ways that might not be entirely within our control. As it grows, the agentic web will inevitably transform the human web—and whether the human web survives this transition is anyone’s guess. For Berners-Lee’s original vision to work, internet users would have had to annotate the pages they built with special tags so that a software agent could understand each element’s meaning—say, “street address” for the part of a physical therapy office’s web page that indicates its location and “appointment types” for the list of services. And so the idea never really caught on. “It’s a lot of labor,” says Eni Mustafaraj, a professor of computer science at Wellesley College. “And the benefits of that were not obvious.” For the next two decades, then, the internet remained a place that put humans first, with the odd Twitter reply bot or web scraper to round things out. Large language models changed that. Unlike the agents that Berners-Lee was imagining, today’s LLM-based agents don’t need any tags to understand which part of the text on a clinic’s site is its address and which details the services it offers. They can search for and process text far faster than any human, and agents with multimodal capabilities can even interpret screenshots of websites and click on specific elements such as hyperlinks and drop-down menus. They’re also just a way more intuitive means of finding information and accomplishing tasks online. Rather than poring over pages of Google results to find a budget-friendly product dupe or a half-remembered meme, why not have Claude or ChatGPT peruse dozens of sites in just a few minutes, guided only by your vague query? Or go one step further and use a personal assistant agent like Muse to hunt down a restaurant reservation or book a flight. As agents flood online spaces, this new user base is changing the web for good. Time magazine, for instance, is publishing versions of its articles that are easier for agents to parse and has started selling ads targeted at them. Companies from Etsy to Expedia have partnered with the major AI firms to build tools that allow agents to interface seamlessly with their services. Despite these early efforts, it’s still tough to tell exactly what forms the agentic web will take and how it will change our online experience. Depending on how it’s designed and who controls access to it, we could be in for something that’s as open and customizable as the web of the early 2000s, only far easier to use. Alternatively, we could be reduced to viewing much of the web through tiny portholes controlled by a few dominant platforms, as independent sites and creators struggle to survive the shift. And as this summer’s series of OpenAI security incidents suggests, the agents might even build their own online networks and resources—whether we want them to or not. How this plays out also depends on us: which parts of our online lives we’re happy to delegate to our agents and where we will still demand a human-centric internet. “There’s a lot we don’t know yet about how users want to use [agents],” says Ajit Varma, head of Firefox at Mozilla. But whatever does happen, the changes will be big. “It’s probably on par with getting a mobile phone,” he says. “I think things are going to change very dramatically.” Building a web for agents There are two ways to approach building the agentic web. The first involves training agents to use browsers like humans—scrolling, clicking, typing—and letting them loose on the web that we’re all used to. The second requires building tools that allow agents to interface with the internet via text and code, their preferred media. That possibility offers more separation between the human and the agentic web: designers can create different experiences for those who use text commands and those who use browsers. When Siva Reddy, a professor of computer science and linguistics at McGill University, began studying LLM agents in 2024, he focused on the first option. “At that time, we thought it should be that the best agent in the world is probably an agent that can use a browser,” he says. Such an agent would integrate seamlessly with the preexisting human web, and its owner could easily supervise it by watching as it navigated familiar interfaces. items.title: SpectRAG: Weighted Chunk Graphs for Token-Budgeted Context Selection in Multi-Hop Retrieval-Augmented Generation
items.description: arXiv:2610.36991v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems ground large language models (LLMs) by retrieving external evidence and conditioning generation on the retrieved context. Although dense retrieval is effective for local semantic matching, independently ranked retrieval can return redundant passages, miss cross-chunk dependencies, and provide incomplete evidence for multi-hop reasoning. We propose SpectRAG, a spectral graph-augmented retrieval framework that combines hybrid candidate seeding, weighted chunk graph construction, graph-based expansion, spectral relevance propagation, and token-budgeted context selection. Document chunks are represented by dense semantic embeddings and graph-spectral coordinates derived from a weighted chunk graph whose edges encode semantic similarity, document adjacency, section hierarchy, shared entities, citation links, and similarity between LLM-generated utility questions. At query time, SpectRAG builds a high-recall seed set using exact inner-product search and hybrid relevance signals, expands it over the chunk graph, re-scores candidates using graph proximity and spectral information, and assembles the final context under a fixed token budget. The goal is not merely to retrieve individually similar chunks, but to construct a context that is relevant, diverse, structurally connected, and sufficient for grounded reasoning. Experiments on MultiHopRAG, UltraDomain, and long-document question-answering settings show that SpectRAG improves broad evidence recovery and achieves competitive generation quality against dense, hybrid, HyDE, LightRAG, and NaiveRAG baselines. The results further indicate that graph-spectral structure is particularly useful for inference-oriented and cross-document retrieval, while highlighting trade-offs in early precision, computational cost, and domain-dependent performance.

items.title: Learning to Reason from Reference Samples Alone: Reinforced Adversarial Learning for Modern LLM Post-Training
items.description: arXiv:2610.38851v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: In many settings where LLM post-training is desirable, high-quality answers are recognizable but difficult to score with explicit rewards. Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) is limited to tasks where an explicit correctness signal is available. Prior adversarial approaches to training reasoning LLMs either complement verifiable rewards with co-trained critics or require reference reasoning traces. We ask whether a co-trained LLM judge can turn reference answers alone into the sole reward for on-policy post-training of reasoning LLMs. We call this method Reinforced Adversarial Learning (RAL). We first validate RAL on three verifiable tasks (integer multiplication, code-based arithmetic-expression synthesis, and SMILES-to-formula translation), using the verifiers only for evaluation. With sufficiently capable judges and enough training, RAL matches direct RLVR. We then apply RAL to scientific abstract generation in two settings. In the first setting, RAL guides the generator to produce abstracts in the scientific domain of the reference abstracts, even though the prompt leaves that domain unspecified. In the second setting, we generate abstracts for U.S. National Institutes of Health grant proposals conditioned on the grant title. Human scientists and an ensemble of LLM judges find our generations harder to distinguish from real abstracts than those of frontier-LLM baselines. These results suggest a path toward post-training reasoning models in scientific and other high-value domains, where increasingly capable judges infer hard-to-specify reward functions from example answers.

items.title: DeFT-RAG: Decomposing Multi-Hop Questions into Self-Contained Sub-Questions with Reusable Answers
items.description: arXiv:2610.37826v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) lets a large language model (LLM) answer questions by retrieving relevant passages from a large corpus. However, RAG struggles with multi-hop questions, which require chaining facts spread across several documents through intermediate entities that the question never mentions. Graph-based RAG methods retrieve once from the entities a question names and so rarely recover the full evidence chain. Iterative RAG methods recover it step by step, but their accuracy is limited by the many tasks they ask the LLM to perform, such as planning the sub-questions, deciding their dependencies, rewriting them as answers arrive, and keeping track of what is known. We propose DeFT-RAG, a RAG framework built on three components. First, DeFT-RAG generates one self-contained sub-question at a time from the original question and the sub-questions answered so far with their answers (QA pairs). Each sub-question names every entity it asks about, which removes the need to plan, track dependencies or rewrite, and lets the LLM focus on a single fine-grained task at a time. Second, DeFT-RAG moves the remaining LLM work outside the LLM: rule-based updates to a QA table that keeps track of what is known, and yes/no decisions made by a fine-tuned lightweight decision model. Third, DeFT-RAG caches the QA pairs and reuses an answer when a later question asks a sub-question with the same meaning. On MuSiQue, 2WikiMultiHopQA and HotpotQA, DeFT-RAG achieves the best accuracy among thirteen baselines with both gpt-4o-mini and Qwen3.6 as the backbone, while giving the LLM fewer input tokens than any other iterative method. With a QA cache shared across 1,000 MuSiQue questions, 23.1% of sub-questions are answered from the cache, which reduces LLM calls by 12.9% without lowering accuracy.
